analysis.one_liner: Opens federal ocean waters to oil and gas drilling and blocks future marine national monuments.
analysis.headline: The bill never came to a vote; it sat in the House Natural Resources Committee until the Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act so presidents could no longer shield most federal ocean waters from oil and gas leasing. It would wipe out existing presidential withdrawals of unleased offshore areas (except marine sanctuaries and existing national monuments), cap any wartime or emergency suspension of drilling to 90-day increments, and prohibit presidents from designating any new ocean national monument under the Antiquities Act. In practice, it would open large stretches of federal waters now off limits to drilling.
analysis.who_benefits: Offshore oil and gas companies, which would gain access to vast unleased federal waters and lose the risk that a president withdraws them. Energy-producing states would gain leasing activity and federal royalties tied to production.

how_it_helps.text: Rescinds existing presidential withdrawals of unleased outer Continental Shelf areas from oil and gas leasing, except in national marine sanctuaries and existing national monuments, making those waters available for drilling.
Limits the President's authority so that no unleased outer Continental Shelf lands may be withdrawn from oil and gas leasing except by an act of Congress.
Prohibits the President from declaring or reserving any ocean waters or lands beneath ocean waters as a national monument, foreclosing a tool previously used to bar drilling in large ocean areas.
Caps any suspension of offshore operations arising from a state of war or declared national emergency to 90-day periods, renewable only in additional 90-day increments.

analysis.who_pays: Coastal communities, commercial and recreational fishing interests, and tourism-dependent economies would bear the risk of new offshore drilling activity, including the danger of spills, near their shores. The public would lose protected ocean areas, and future presidents and Congresses would lose a low-cost tool to protect them.

drawbacks.text: Rescinding existing withdrawals would open currently protected waters to drilling, exposing coastal fisheries, beaches, and tourism economies to the risk of spills and industrial activity.
Blocking new marine national monuments and requiring an act of Congress to protect any other offshore area makes protecting federal waters far harder, even in response to specific risks.

Supporters would argue the bill simply curbs unilateral executive power and expands domestic energy production and federal royalties; an honest weighing of that position must still note it removes protection from areas chosen for their environmental or economic value rather than through any case-by-case review.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains accrue narrowly to companies that would lease newly opened federal waters, while the risks — spills, damage to fisheries, loss of protected ocean areas — fall on coastal communities and the public with no compensating safeguard. The bill's one structural argument, limiting presidential power, does not account for the loss of emergency or long-term protection tools it would eliminate.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and then to two of its subcommittees, never got a hearing or markup, and died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Rep. Dave Brat (R-VA) introduced the OCEAN Act on April 26, 2017 with 22 Republican original cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources, and days later to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources and the Subcommittee on Water, Power and Oceans.
No further action appears in the record — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — and the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 without the bill advancing.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coastal communities, fishing and tourism interests, and ocean protection generally are better off because the bill died: existing presidential withdrawals of offshore waters stayed in force and no new drilling access was created. Offshore drillers gained nothing from the outcome.

for.name: Rep. Dave Brat
for.what_they_did: Introduced the OCEAN Act to open outer Continental Shelf waters to oil and gas leasing and block new ocean national monuments.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral and never reported it out; the record shows no hearing, markup, or vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 23 sponsors and cosponsors were House Republicans; no Democratic support appears in the record and no votes were ever taken.

industries.note: The bill would give drillers access to large unleased federal waters now off limits and remove presidential power to withdraw them, while the spill and industrial-activity risks fall on coastal communities and the public.
Opening protected waters to drilling and blocking new ocean monuments would expose fishing grounds and sensitive habitats to drilling activity and spill risk.
Beach and coastal tourism depends on clean waters and shorelines; expanded drilling would put that at risk with no direct offsetting benefit to those regions.
